```{r}
library(datavolley)
library(tidyverse)
library(igraph)
library(ggraph)
library(knitr)
library(patchwork)
library(ggrepel)
```

# Research question 

"Social Network Analysis in Elite Volleyball: Quantifying Tactical Predictability and Ball Distribution Adaptability via Network Metrics"

## 1. Data cleaning and counting pass connection

```{r}
match_data <- dv_read("new_test.dvw")
plays <- match_data$plays

transitions_base <- plays %>%
  filter(!is.na(player_name), !is.na(skill)) %>%
  # group by individual point to keep sequence analysis within the same rally
  group_by(match_id, set_number, point_id) %>%
  # identify the next touch: player, team, and skill
  mutate(
    next_player    = lead(player_name),
    next_team      = lead(team),
    next_skill     = lead(skill),
    reception_eval = lag(evaluation)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

network_data <- transitions_base %>%
  # keep only valid teammate connections (from Reception/Dig to Set or from Set to Attack)
  filter(
    team == next_team,
    player_name != next_player,
    (skill %in% c("Reception", "Dig") & next_skill == "Set") |
    (skill == "Set" & next_skill == "Attack")
  ) %>%
  count(team, from = player_name, to = next_player, name = "weight")
```

## 2. The Network
We model team dynamics as a directed weighted graph $G = (V, E)$, where nodes are players and directed edges $(i,j)$ represent consecutive touches between teammates, weighted by touch frequency $w_{ij}$.

```{r}
draw_match_network <- function(data, team_name, team_color, main_title = "Match Network", sub_title = NULL) {
  # filter data for the single team and keep last names only
  team_edges <- data %>% 
    filter(team == team_name) %>% 
    mutate(
      from = word(from, -1),
      to = word(to, -1)
    ) %>% 
    select(from, to, weight)
  
  # create graph object
  g <- graph_from_data_frame(team_edges, directed = TRUE)
  
  # draw network plot
  ggraph(g, layout = "circle") +
    geom_edge_arc(
      aes(width = weight, label = weight),
      strength = 0.15, color = team_color, alpha = 0.6,
      arrow = arrow(length = unit(2.5, "mm"), type = "closed"),
      end_cap = circle(5, "mm"),
      label_size = 3.2
    ) +
    scale_edge_width(range = c(0.5, 2.5), guide = "none") +
    geom_node_point(size = 6, fill = "white", color = team_color, shape = 21, stroke = 1.3) +
    geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
    theme_graph() +
    labs(
      title = paste(main_title, ":", team_name),
      subtitle = sub_title
    )
}

teams <- unique(network_data$team)

draw_match_network(network_data, teams[1], "blue")
draw_match_network(network_data, teams[2], "red")
```

## 3. Hub centrality
By evaluating incoming (in-degree) and outgoing (out-degree) flow metrics, we quantify how ball distribution is allocated across team members. This analysis validates the setter’s structural role as the primary network hub while identifying key offensive targets (high in-degree) and play-building anchors (high out-degree).

```{r}
calculate_hub_centrality <- function(net_df, team_name) {
  df_team <- net_df %>% filter(team == team_name)
  
  # incoming flows to the player
  in_edges <- df_team %>% 
    mutate(to = word(to, -1)) %>% 
    count(player_name = to, wt = weight, name = "in_degree")
  
  # outgoing flows from the player
  out_edges <- df_team %>% 
    mutate(from = word(from, -1)) %>% 
    count(player_name = from, wt = weight, name = "out_degree")

  # merge incoming/outgoing degrees and compute total flow percentage
  full_join(in_edges, out_edges, by = "player_name") %>%
    mutate(
      in_degree  = coalesce(in_degree, 0L),
      out_degree = coalesce(out_degree, 0L),
      total_degree = in_degree + out_degree,
      total_flow_pct = round((total_degree / sum(total_degree)) * 100, 1)
    ) %>%
    arrange(desc(total_degree))
}

(hub_team_A <- calculate_hub_centrality(network_data, teams[1]))
(hub_team_B <- calculate_hub_centrality(network_data, teams[2]))
```

## 4. Eigenvector Centrality

While degree centrality counts individual connections, **Eigenvector Centrality** quantifies a node's influence by taking into account the centrality of its neighbors. In a directed sports network $G = (V, E)$, the eigenvector centrality $x_i$ of player $i$ is proportional to the sum of the centralities of all players connected to them:

$$\lambda x_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} A_{ij} x_j$$

where $A_{ij}$ represents the weighted adjacency matrix (touch volume) and $\lambda$ is the largest eigenvalue of $A$. High values identify key players operating within the primary hub-and-spoke sequence of the team's build-up play.

```{r}
calculate_eigenvector_centrality <- function(net_df, team_name) {
  team_edges <- net_df %>% 
    filter(team == team_name) %>% 
    mutate(
      from = word(from, -1),
      to = word(to, -1)
    ) %>% 
    select(from, to, weight)
  
  g <- graph_from_data_frame(team_edges, directed = TRUE)
  
  ev_scores <- eigen_centrality(g, weights = E(g)$weight, directed = TRUE)$vector

  data.frame(
    player_name = names(ev_scores),
    eigen_centrality = round(ev_scores, 4),
    team = team_name,
    row.names = NULL 
  ) %>%
    arrange(desc(eigen_centrality))
}

(ev_team_A <- calculate_eigenvector_centrality(network_data, teams[1]))
(ev_team_B <- calculate_eigenvector_centrality(network_data, teams[2]))
```


## 5. Attacker Workload Distribution
Isolates setter-to-attacker transitions (Set -> Attack) to quantify the outgoing flow from the setter,
measuring the exact offensive workload and distribution strategy across key hitters.

```{r}
set_attacks <- transitions_base %>%
  filter(team == next_team, skill == "Set", next_skill == "Attack") %>%
  mutate(
    setter       = word(player_name, -1),
    attacker     = word(next_player, -1),
    team_score   = if_else(team == home_team, home_team_score, visiting_team_score),
    opp_score    = if_else(team == home_team, visiting_team_score, home_team_score),
    score_margin = team_score - opp_score,
    game_phase   = if_else(score_margin <= -3, "Trailing", "Normal_Leading"),
    pass_quality = if_else(
      reception_eval %in% c("Perfect pass", "Positive, attack", "Positive pass", "#", "+"), 
      "Perfect", 
      "Non_Perfect"
    )
  )

# isolate setter -> attacker transitions
attacker_workload <- set_attacks %>%
  count(team, attacker, name = "sets_received") %>%
  group_by(team) %>%
  mutate(pct = round((sets_received / sum(sets_received)) * 100, 1)) %>%
  ungroup()

ggplot(attacker_workload, aes(x = pct, y = reorder(attacker, pct), fill = team)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(pct, "%")), 
    hjust = -0.15,          
    fontface = "bold", 
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~team, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 45)) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Attacker Workload Distribution (Out-Degree)",
    x = "Percentage of Sets (%)", 
    y = "Attacker"
  )
```

```{r}
# sub-network

attacks <- set_attacks %>%
  count(team, from = setter, to = attacker, name = "weight")

teams <- unique(attacks$team)

draw_match_network(attacks, teams[1], "blue", main_title = "Distribution Network", sub_title = "Pass volume: Setter -> Attackers")
draw_match_network(attacks, teams[2], "red", main_title = "Distribution Network", sub_title = "Pass volume: Setter -> Attackers")
```

## 6. Workload vs. Attack Efficiency Analysis
To evaluate the tactical efficacy of setter distribution strategies, we cross-referenced each attacker's workload percentage ($\text{Set Share %}$) with their scoring efficiency ($\text{Kill%}$). This dual-metric approach reveals whether high-volume targets justified their workload or suffered from predictable blocking and fatigue.

```{r}
workload_summary <- attacks %>%
  group_by(team, attacker = to) %>%
  summarise(sets_received = sum(weight), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(team) %>%
  mutate(pct = round((sets_received / sum(sets_received)) * 100, 1)) %>%
  ungroup()

# attack efficiency calculation (Kill %) 
attack_summary <- plays %>%
  filter(skill == "Attack", !is.na(player_name)) %>%
  mutate(player_name = word(player_name, -1)) %>%
  group_by(team, player_name) %>%
  summarise(
    total_attacks = n(),
    kills = sum(evaluation == "Winning attack", na.rm = TRUE),
    kill_pct = round((kills / total_attacks) * 100, 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# merge
data_plot_clean <- workload_summary %>%
  inner_join(attack_summary, by = c("team", "attacker" = "player_name")) %>%
  mutate(
    # extracts last name only to fit labels cleanly
    label_name = word(attacker, -1)
  )

ggplot(data_plot_clean, aes(x = pct, y = kill_pct, color = team)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_text_repel(
    aes(label = label_name),
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 3.8,
    box.padding = 0.6,
    point.padding = 0.3,
    force = 4,
    max.overlaps = Inf,
    min.segment.length = 0,
    segment.color = "grey60",
    segment.size = 0.4
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~team) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Workload (%) vs Attack Efficiency (Kill %)",
    x = "Share of Sets Received (%) [Workload]",
    y = "Attack Success Rate (%) [Kill %]"
  )
```

## 7. Shannon Entropy

To quantify the tactical predictability of setter decision-making under match stress, we implemented a metric based on **Relative Shannon Entropy** ($H_{rel}$). Entropy measures the degree of randomness or diversity in ball distribution across available attackers:

$$H_{rel} = \frac{-\sum_{i=1}^{k} p_i \log_2(p_i)}{\log_2(k)}$$

where $p_i$ represents the proportion of sets received by attacker $i$, and $k$ is the total number of active attack options. 

- $H_{rel} = 1$ indicates maximum unpredictability (an perfectly even distribution across all options).
- $H_{rel} \to 0$ indicates high predictability (over-reliance on a single primary target).

By comparing $H_{rel}$ during standard play (`Normal_Leading`) versus high-stress scenarios (`Trailing`), we evaluate whether score-induced pressure causes setters to narrow their distribution patterns and rely on predictable fallback targets ($\Delta H = H_{\text{Trailing}} - H_{\text{Normal}}$).

```{r}
calculate_entropy <- function(counts) {
  p <- counts / sum(counts)
  p <- p[p > 0]
  k <- length(p)
  if (k <= 1) return(0)
  
  h_abs <- -sum(p * log2(p))
  h_max <- log2(k)
  
  return(round(h_abs / h_max, 4))
}

main_setters <- set_attacks %>%
  count(team, setter) %>%
  group_by(team) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 1) %>%
  pull(setter)

total_entropy <- set_attacks %>%
  filter(setter %in% main_setters) %>%
  group_by(team, setter, game_phase, attacker) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop_last") %>%
  summarise(H_rel = calculate_entropy(n), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = game_phase, values_from = H_rel) %>%
  mutate(
    Normal_Leading = coalesce(Normal_Leading, 0),
    Trailing       = coalesce(Trailing, 0),
    Delta_H        = round(Trailing - Normal_Leading, 4)
  )

print(total_entropy)
```

## 8. Frobenius Distance

To assess how reception quality impacts distribution structure, we computed the **Frobenius Distance** ($D_F$) between two normalized adjacency matrices representing setter choices under **Perfect** vs. **Non-Perfect** pass conditions:

$$D_F = \| A_{\text{Perfect}} - A_{\text{Non-Perfect}} \|_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i} \sum_{j} \left| a_{ij}^{(\text{Perf})} - a_{ij}^{(\text{Non-Perf})} \right|^2}$$

A low Frobenius Distance ($D_F \approx 0$) indicates high structural stability, meaning the setter maintains her intended tactical distribution regardless of pass quality. Conversely, a higher $D_F$ value highlights tactical constraint, where poor reception forces the setter to abandon complex offensive patterns and rely on predictable fallback options (e.g., high balls to the high-volume outside hitter).

```{r}
calculate_frobenius <- function(df_data, team_name) {
  df_sub <- df_data %>% filter(team == team_name)
  
  # matrix for perfect pass
  m_perf <- table(df_sub$setter[df_sub$pass_quality == "Perfect"], 
                  df_sub$attacker[df_sub$pass_quality == "Perfect"])
  
  # matrix for non-perfect Pass
  m_imperf <- table(df_sub$setter[df_sub$pass_quality == "Non_Perfect"], 
                    df_sub$attacker[df_sub$pass_quality == "Non_Perfect"])
  
  # matrix normalization
  if (sum(m_perf) > 0) m_perf <- m_perf / sum(m_perf)
  if (sum(m_imperf) > 0) m_imperf <- m_imperf / sum(m_imperf)
  
  all_setters   <- union(rownames(m_perf), rownames(m_imperf))
  all_attackers <- union(colnames(m_perf), colnames(m_imperf))
  
  mat1 <- matrix(0, nrow = length(all_setters), ncol = length(all_attackers),
                 dimnames = list(all_setters, all_attackers))
  mat2 <- mat1
  
  mat1[rownames(m_perf), colnames(m_perf)]     <- m_perf
  mat2[rownames(m_imperf), colnames(m_imperf)] <- m_imperf
  
  # frobenius distance
  d_f <- norm(mat1 - mat2, type = "F")
  return(round(d_f, 4))
}

teams <- unique(set_attacks$team)

frobenius_res <- data.frame(
  team = teams,
  Frobenius_Distance = sapply(teams, function(t) calculate_frobenius(set_attacks, t))
)

print(frobenius_res)
```

```{r}
# drew Frobenius comparison network 

draw_frobenius_network <- function(df_data, team_name, pass_qual, team_color = "navy") {
  edges <- df_data %>%
    filter(team == team_name, pass_quality == pass_qual, setter %in% main_setters) %>%
    group_by(setter, attacker) %>%
    summarise(weight_raw = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(weight = round((weight_raw / sum(weight_raw)) * 100, 1)) %>%
    select(from = setter, to = attacker, weight)
  
  if (nrow(edges) == 0) return(NULL)
  
  all_nodes <- unique(c(edges$from, edges$to))
  g <- graph_from_data_frame(edges, vertices = data.frame(name = all_nodes), directed = TRUE)
 
  ggraph(g, layout = "circle") +
    geom_edge_arc(
      aes(width = weight, label = paste0(weight, "%")),
      strength = 0.2, color = team_color, alpha = 0.7,
      arrow = arrow(length = unit(3, 'mm'), type = "closed"),
      end_cap = circle(6, 'mm'), label_size = 3.5, label_colour = "black"
    ) +
    scale_edge_width(range = c(0.8, 3.0), guide = "none") +
    geom_node_point(size = 8, fill = "white", color = team_color, shape = 21, stroke = 1.5) +
    geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, fontface = "bold", size = 3.8, box.padding = 0.8) +
    theme_graph() +
    labs(
      title = paste(team_name, "-", pass_qual, "Pass Network"),
      subtitle = "Set distribution percentage (%)"
    )
}

(p_milano_perf   <- draw_frobenius_network(set_attacks, teams[1], "Perfect", "blue"))
(p_milano_imperf <- draw_frobenius_network(set_attacks, teams[1], "Non_Perfect", "red"))

(p_firenze_perf   <- draw_frobenius_network(set_attacks, teams[2], "Perfect", "blue"))
(p_firenze_imperf <- draw_frobenius_network(set_attacks, teams[2], "Non_Perfect", "red"))
```
